title: LED Resistor Calculator
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Clocks and Watches with AI
description: Choose an LED color, a 3.3 V or 5 V supply, and a standard resistor to see the LED current, its brightness, a warning above 20 mA, and the resistor you would need for 10 mA.

learningObjectives: Apply the current-limiting formula to calculate LED current and the resistor needed for a target current.
Analyze how resistor value, supply voltage, and LED color change the current and brightness.
Choose a safe standard resistor value for an LED on a 3.3 V Pico pin.
prerequisites: Read the Current Limiting and LED Basics sections of Chapter 2.

accessibility.notes: Screen-reader description provided; all controls are standard HTML elements.

keyQuestions: What happens to the current if you halve the resistor?
Why does a blue LED barely light from a 3.3 V pin with a 330 Ω resistor?
Which standard resistor would you use for a red LED at 10 mA from 5 V?
commonMisconceptions: Using the full supply voltage instead of the leftover voltage (supply minus forward voltage) in the formula.
Thinking a bigger resistor makes the LED brighter.
Thinking an LED can be connected without a resistor because it "has its own voltage."
assessmentOpportunities: Students correctly calculate the resistor needed for a given LED color, supply, and target current.
Students explain why a smaller resistor makes the LED brighter and when that becomes unsafe.
Students explain why blue and white LEDs need smaller resistors on a 3.3 V pin.
pedagogical.interactionPattern: Parameter exploration with live readout and safety warning
